title: Expressions, operators, and equality
runtime: Modern evergreen browser or Node.js with ES modules. Run fragments in browser DevTools or a small .js file unless the example says otherwise.

objectives.text: Use arithmetic, logical, comparison, and assignment operators.
Prefer strict equality and understand Object.is.

learningFlow: Explain the result in your own words
Apply the idea in a different problem
Review after two and seven days

diagnostic.question: Can you explain the main purpose of expressions, operators, and equality before reading?
diagnostic.answer: A complete answer should name the problem it solves, the values or control flow involved, and one mistake to avoid.

sections.title: Expressions produce values
sections.body: An expression evaluates to a value: 2 + 3, user.name, and isReady ? "Go" : "Wait" are expressions. A statement performs a larger action, such as if, for, return, or a variable declaration. JSX braces accept expressions, which is why a conditional expression works there but an if statement does not fit directly.

sections.title: Operators combine or change values
sections.body: Arithmetic operators calculate numbers, comparison operators produce booleans, and assignment stores a result. && and || short-circuit: they stop when the result is known and return an operand rather than always returning true or false. Operator precedence controls grouping, but parentheses make important intent visible.

sections.title: Equality has rules
sections.body: === compares without converting types, so 0 === "0" is false. == performs coercion and can hide an input problem, so use it only when you can explain the intended conversion. Objects compare by identity, not by matching contents. Object.is differs for NaN and signed zero and is used by some React comparisons.

sections.title: Name important conditions
sections.body: Boolean logic is easier to test when each part has one meaning. Instead of a long expression in JSX, calculate names such as hasItems and canCheckout. De Morgan’s laws explain how negation changes groups, but straightforward positive conditions are usually easier for a learner to verify.

sections.title: Why this matters in React
sections.body: Expressions, operators, and equality is part of the JavaScript model React code already uses. Components, event handlers, state updates, list rendering, and data requests become easier to reason about when this concept is understood without framework shortcuts. Practise the JavaScript behavior first, then identify the same rule in JSX or a component.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain expressions, operators, and equality to a junior developer.
interviewQuestions.answer: Distinguish expressions from statements. Use arithmetic, logical, comparison, and assignment operators. Prefer strict equality and understand Object.is. Build readable boolean expressions.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Show a small example and one common mistake.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you prove that code using expressions, operators, and equality behaves correctly?
interviewQuestions.answer: State the expected value or control flow first, test normal and boundary cases, and inspect the actual runtime result. Explain the JavaScript rule behind the evidence.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which edge case would you test first?

interviewQuestions.question: Where can expressions, operators, and equality affect React code?
interviewQuestions.answer: It can affect values, callbacks, rendering decisions, updates, or data flow. The exact connection depends on the concept; the important step is to reason from JavaScript behavior before blaming React.

mastery.policy: Reading or opening a solution is guided exposure, not mastery. Save an attempt, solve again without help, explain the rule, and transfer it to a new problem.

commonMistakes.symptom: Code using expressions, operators, and equality produces a surprising value.
commonMistakes.cause: The result was run before the value, type, scope, identity, or control flow was predicted.
commonMistakes.fix: Reduce the case, write the expected result, and apply the exact rule from the matching section.

commonMistakes.symptom: A learner copies syntax but cannot adapt it.
commonMistakes.cause: The example was memorized without explaining why it works.
commonMistakes.fix: Change the data and names, predict again, and explain which behavior must stay the same.

commonMistakes.symptom: A React problem is blamed on React immediately.
commonMistakes.cause: The underlying JavaScript behavior was not isolated first.
commonMistakes.fix: Reproduce the value or function behavior in a small JavaScript example, then reconnect it to the component.
